---
title: "Plotting Causal Graphs"
knitr:
  opts_chunk:
    collapse: true
    comment: "#>"
---

`cgraph_plot()` draws a `cgraph` with
[grid](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/grid/html/00Index.html)
graphics. For node placement, you can use the layouts provided by
[Sugiyama.jl](https://github.com/BjarkeHautop/Sugiyama.jl) or
[NetworkLayout.jl](https://github.com/JuliaGraphs/NetworkLayout.jl)^[The
compiled library uses [a fork of
NetworkLayout.jl](https://github.com/BjarkeHautop/NetworkLayout.jl/tree/trim-compat),
since the released version does not compile with `juliac --trim=safe`.], or
provide your own layout:

```{r}
#| label: setup

library(CausalStructures)
```

::: {.callout-note title="General-purpose by design"}
There are many conventions for drawing causal graphs. For example, you might box
conditioned variables, dash latent variables, draw `<->` as a dashed arc, or use
different colors for exposures and outcomes.

`cgraph_plot()` does not impose any of these conventions by default. Instead,
you can use the style functions, global defaults, and layouts to choose the
conventions that make sense for your application[^1].

[^1]: `plot_options()` presets for common conventions are also welcome as PRs!
:::

## Basic usage

You can pass any `cgraph` to `cgraph_plot()`, and all edge marks are supported:

```{r}
#| label: edge-marks

unknown <- cgraph("A <-> B o-> C o-- A", class = "UNKNOWN")
cgraph_plot(unknown)
```

As an example, here is the DAG from Figure 6.5 of Peters, Janzing and Schölkopf
(2017):

```{r}
#| label: basic-dag

dag <- cgraph(
  "C --> X, A --> X + K, X --> F + D, K --> Y, D --> Y + G, Y --> H"
)
cgraph_plot(dag)
```

`cgraph_plot()` returns a `cgraph_plot` object, which is drawn when it is
printed. At the console that happens automatically; inside a function or loop,
call `print()` on it. `plot(dag)` is a shortcut that builds the plot and draws
it right away.

## Styling a plot

Before a plot is drawn, you can add styling to it step by step, chained with
`|>`:

```{r}
#| label: compose

cgraph_plot(dag) |>
  style_edges(col = "gray60") |>
  style_nodes(fill = "lightskyblue", nodes = "Y") |>
  style_edges(col = "#DC143C", lwd = 2, from = "K", to = "Y")
```

There are five style functions:

- **[`style_nodes()`](#styling-nodes)** styles the nodes in `nodes`.
- **[`style_edges()`](#styling-edges)** styles the edges joining a node in
  `from` to a node in `to`, optionally of a given `type`.
- **[`style_labels()`](#labels)** styles the node labels in `nodes`, and
  **`label_nodes()`** sets their text.
- **[`style_title()`](#titles)** styles the title.

Each call styles only the nodes or edges it selects; leaving out a selector
selects everything. If two calls set the same field, the later one wins, so you
can start with a style for all edges, as above, and then single some out.

Since the selectors are node sets, you can pass the results of query functions
straight in. For example, to highlight the parents of `Y` and dash the edges
into it:

```{r}
#| label: compose-queries

cgraph_plot(dag) |>
  style_nodes(fill = "lightskyblue", nodes = parents(dag, "Y")) |>
  style_edges(lty = "dashed", to = "Y", type = "-->")
```

A style function also accepts a graph directly, starting the plot with the
default layout, so `dag |> style_nodes(fill = "gold")` works too.

If you want to set defaults for an entire project, you can use `plot_options()`,
with a list of fields for each of `node_style`, `edge_style`, `label_style` and
`title_style`. The style functions still take precedence, and
`plot_options(plot_default_options())` resets to the built-in defaults:

```r
plot_options(node_style = list(fill = "lightblue"), edge_style = list(lwd = 2))
```

`cgraph_grob()` gives the grid grob of a plot, if you want to draw it yourself
with `grid::grid.draw()`, for example in a viewport of a larger figure.

## Layout {#plot-layouts}

The `layout` argument controls where the nodes are placed. It defaults to
`"sugiyama"` for a `DAG`, and to `"stress"` otherwise.

```{r}
#| label: layout-stress

cgraph_plot(dag, layout = "stress")
```

You can use these names for the built-in layouts. `"sugiyama"` comes from
[Sugiyama.jl](https://github.com/BjarkeHautop/Sugiyama.jl), while the others
come from [NetworkLayout.jl](https://github.com/JuliaGraphs/NetworkLayout.jl),
as in CausalStructures.jl; see `?cgraph_layout` for details:

  | `layout`       | Algorithm                           |
  | -------------- | ----------------------------------- |
  | `"sugiyama"`   | Sugiyama (layered) layout           |
  | `"stress"`     | Stress majorization                 |
  | `"spring"`     | Fruchterman-Reingold force-directed |
  | `"sfdp"`       | Scalable force-directed placement   |
  | `"spectral"`   | Spectral layout                     |
  | `"shell"`      | Nodes evenly spaced on a circle     |
  | `"squaregrid"` | Square grid                         |

`"stress"`, `"spring"` and `"sfdp"` start from random positions; `seed` (default
`1`) makes them reproducible.

For `"sugiyama"`, `direction` (`"right"`, the default, `"down"`, `"up"`, or
`"left"`) sets which way the layers flow:

```{r}
#| label: layout-direction

cgraph_plot(dag, direction = "down")
```

If you want to place the nodes yourself, you can pass explicit positions instead
of a name. You can either use a named list of `c(x, y)` pairs keyed by node
name, or a `data.frame` with `name`, `x`, and `y` columns:

```{r}
#| label: layout-fixed

cgraph_plot(
  dag,
  layout = list(
    A = c(0, 1),
    C = c(0, -1),
    K = c(1, 1),
    X = c(1, -1),
    D = c(2, -1),
    F = c(2, -2),
    Y = c(3, 0),
    G = c(3, 1),
    H = c(4, 0)
  )
)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Tweaking a layout by hand"}
You can compute a starting layout using `cgraph_layout()`, and then manually
adjust a few nodes:

```{r}
#| label: layout-tweak

positions <- cgraph_layout(dag, method = "stress")
positions[positions$name == "G", c("x", "y")] <- c(1, 1.5)
cgraph_plot(dag, layout = positions)
```
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Sugiyama positions without Sugiyama routing"}
Sugiyama.jl implements its own routing using dummy nodes. If you prefer the
automatic Bezier-curve routing used otherwise, you can compute the Sugiyama
positions with `cgraph_layout()` and pass those instead:

```{r}
#| label: sugiyama-positions

dag_layered <- cgraph("A --> X, A --> B, X --> Y, B --> Y, A --> Y")
cgraph_plot(dag_layered, layout = cgraph_layout(dag_layered, "sugiyama"))
```
:::

## Styling nodes

`style_nodes()` takes these fields:

  | Field       | Default           | Controls                                                 |
  | ----------- | ----------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- |
  | `fill`      | `"white"`         | fill color                                               |
  | `col`       | `"black"`         | border color                                             |
  | `lwd`       | `1`               | border line width                                        |
  | `linestyle` | solid             | border line style (any `lty`)                            |
  | `shape`     | `"circle"`        | node outline shape                                       |
  | `radius`    | `NULL` (text-fit) | size of each node (mm)                                   |
  | `padding`   | `2`               | clearance (mm) around each label when `radius` is `NULL` |
  | `size`      | `1`               | multiplier on the computed node size                     |

Combine color, border, and shape to highlight a node:

```{r}
#| label: node-highlight

cgraph_plot(dag) |>
  style_nodes(fill = "lightblue", col = "navy") |>
  style_nodes(fill = "salmon", col = "#DC143C", nodes = "A") |>
  style_nodes(shape = "square", nodes = "K")
```

You can set `shape` to `"circle"` (the default), `"square"`, `"ellipse"`, or
`"rect"`. The latter two are mainly useful when you want to fit an oblong label.
You can also use `linestyle` to style the border, for example to mark a latent
variable:

```{r}
#| label: node-linestyle

dag |> style_nodes(linestyle = "dashed", col = "gray50", nodes = "X")
```

If you only want to draw the node names, you can make the fill and the border
transparent. Edges still stop at the (now invisible) node boundary, so you can
use `"rect"` with a smaller `padding` to bring the arrowheads closer to the
text:

```{r}
#| label: node-transparent

dag |>
  style_nodes(
    fill = "transparent",
    col = "transparent",
    shape = "rect",
    padding = 1
  )
```

### Text-fit node sizing

By default (`radius = NULL`), nodes are sized to fit their labels:

```{r}
#| label: text-fit

longlabels <- cgraph("Exposure --> Mediator --> Y_outcome")
longlabels |> style_nodes(shape = "ellipse", nodes = "Exposure")
```

If you want to control the size yourself, you can set `radius` explicitly:

```{r}
#| label: fixed-radius

dag |> style_nodes(radius = 6)
```

## Styling edges

`style_edges()` selects the edges joining a node in `from` to a node in `to`, in
either direction. `type` keeps only the edges with the given notation, read from
`from` to `to`, so it also fixes the direction:

  | Call                                            | Styles                        |
  | ----------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------- |
  | `style_edges(p, ...)`                           | every edge                    |
  | `style_edges(p, ..., from = "X")`               | every edge touching `X`       |
  | `style_edges(p, ..., from = "X", type = "-->")` | the edges out of `X`          |
  | `style_edges(p, ..., to = "X", type = "-->")`   | the edges into `X`            |
  | `style_edges(p, ..., from = "A", to = "X")`     | the edges between `A` and `X` |
  | `style_edges(p, ..., type = "<->")`             | every bidirected edge         |

The notations are `"-->"`, `"<--"`, `"---"`, `"<->"`, `"o->"`, `"<-o"`, `"o--"`,
`"--o"`, and `"o-o"`. `style_edges()` takes these fields:

  | Field         | Default                   | Controls                                   |
  | ------------- | ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
  | `col`         | `"black"`                 | line / marker color                        |
  | `fill`        | `NULL` (the edge's `col`) | arrowhead fill color                       |
  | `lwd`         | `1`                       | line width                                 |
  | `lty`         | solid                     | line style                                 |
  | `gap`         | `0`                       | gap (mm) at edge ends                      |
  | `curvature`   | `NULL`                    | how far the edge bows                      |
  | `path`        | `NULL`                    | explicit waypoints for an edge's route     |
  | `arrow_size`  | `3`                       | length (mm) of arrowhead triangles         |
  | `circle_size` | `1.5`                     | radius (mm) of open-circle (`o`) endpoints |

Let's style some edges by type:

```{r}
#| label: edge-per-type

admg <- cgraph("X --> Y, X <-> Z, Z --> Y", class = "ADMG")

cgraph_plot(admg) |>
  style_edges(col = "steelblue", type = "-->") |>
  style_edges(col = "#DC143C", lwd = 2.5, type = "<->")
```

`fill` controls the arrowhead's fill color. By default (`NULL`), it uses the
edge's resolved `col`, so arrowheads are solid. If you want hollow, outline-only
arrowheads, pass `NA`:

```{r}
#| label: edge-fill

dag |> style_edges(fill = NA)
```

`lty` styles the edge line itself. For example, you can use it to dash `<->`
edges:

```{r}
#| label: edge-lty

admg |> style_edges(lty = "dashed", type = "<->")
```

If you prefer some space between each end of an edge and the node border, you
can set `gap`:

```{r}
#| label: edge-gap

dag |> style_edges(gap = 1)
```

### Parallel edges

If an `ADMG` has both `X --> Y` and `X <-> Y`, `from = "X", to = "Y"` selects
both edges. If you need to distinguish them, add `type`:

```{r}
#| label: edge-by-type

shared <- cgraph("X --> Y, X <-> Y", class = "ADMG")

cgraph_plot(shared) |>
  style_edges(col = "steelblue") |>
  style_edges(col = "#DC143C", from = "X", to = "Y", type = "<->")
```

Notice that the two edges between `X` and `Y` are automatically curved apart, so
they don't overlap.

### Curvature and automatic routing

`curvature` bows an edge into an arc instead of drawing it straight. Positive
values bow the edge to the left when travelling from its first node to its
second (as listed by `edges()`), while negative values bow it to the right.

```{r}
#| label: curvature

admg |> style_edges(curvature = -0.3, type = "<->")
```

If a straight edge would pass too close to a non-incident node, it is
automatically bent around that node with a Bezier curve. Edges with nothing in
the way are always drawn straight.

```{r}
#| label: auto-routing

detour <- cgraph("A --> X + Y, X --> Y")

cgraph_plot(detour, layout = list(A = c(0, 0), X = c(1, 0), Y = c(2, 0)))
```

If you want to disable this automatic routing for a particular edge, you can set
its `curvature` to `0`:

```{r}
#| label: no-routing

cgraph_plot(detour, layout = list(A = c(0, 0), X = c(1, 0), Y = c(2, 0))) |>
  style_edges(curvature = 0, from = "A", to = "Y")
```

### Explicit edge paths

Edges are normally drawn as straight lines unless automatic routing is needed.
If you want to control the path yourself, you can set `path` and provide
intermediate points for the edge, in the coordinates of the layout. For example,
the edge `K --> Y` below is drawn through the point `(0.5, -0.25)`:

```{r}
#| label: edge-path

positions <- cgraph_layout(dag, method = "stress")

cgraph_plot(dag, layout = positions) |>
  style_edges(path = c(0.5, -0.25), from = "K", to = "Y")
```

For several points, `path` can also be a two-column matrix, a `data.frame` with
`x` and `y` columns, or a list of `c(x, y)` points, listed from the node in
`from` to the node in `to`.

## Labels and titles

### Labels

By default, each node is labelled with its own name. If you want different
labels, you can set them with `label_nodes()`. Node sizing takes multi-line
labels into account, so the nodes grow to fit:

```{r}
#| label: labels

cgraph("A0 --> L1 --> A1 --> Y, A0 --> Y + A1") |>
  label_nodes(
    A0 = "Treatment\nat baseline",
    L1 = "Confounder\nat time 1",
    A1 = "Treatment\nat time 1"
  )
```

`style_labels()` styles the label text of the nodes in `nodes`:

  | Field        | Default   | Controls    |
  | ------------ | --------- | ----------- |
  | `col`        | `"black"` | text color  |
  | `fontsize`   | `10`      | font size   |
  | `fontface`   | `"plain"` | font face   |
  | `fontfamily` | `""`      | font family |

```{r}
#| label: label-style

cgraph_plot(dag) |>
  style_labels(fontsize = 13) |>
  style_labels(col = "#DC143C", nodes = "A")
```

### Edge labels

Edge labels are set with `style_edges()`, so they select edges in the same way
as [edge styling](#styling-edges).

  | Field              | Default   | Controls                                                                  |
  | ------------------ | --------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
  | `label`            | `NULL`    | text drawn along the edge                                                 |
  | `label_col`        | `"black"` | edge label text color                                                     |
  | `label_fontsize`   | `9`       | edge label font size                                                      |
  | `label_fontface`   | `"plain"` | edge label font face                                                      |
  | `label_fontfamily` | `""`      | edge label font family                                                    |
  | `label_shift`      | `0.5`     | position along the edge, 0 (first node) to 1 (second node)                |
  | `label_distance`   | `NULL`    | perpendicular gap (mm) from the edge; `NULL` scales with `label_fontsize` |
  | `label_rotation`   | `NULL`    | text angle in degrees; `NULL` follows the edge's own angle                |

Let's add a label to the edge `K --> Y`:

```{r}
#| label: edge-label

dag |> style_edges(label = "hello", from = "K", to = "Y")
```

By default, the label follows the edge's angle. You can use `label_shift` and
`label_distance` to move it along or away from the edge:

```{r}
#| label: edge-label-shift

cgraph_plot(dag) |>
  style_edges(label_shift = 0.75, label_distance = 4) |>
  style_edges(label = "hi", from = "K", to = "Y")
```

If an edge is steep or curved, following its angle can make the label hard to
read. You can use `label_rotation` to give it a fixed angle instead:

```{r}
#| label: edge-label-rotation

cgraph_plot(dag) |>
  style_edges(
    label = "steep",
    label_rotation = 0,
    label_distance = 6,
    label_col = "#DC143C",
    from = "A",
    to = "X"
  ) |>
  style_edges(label = "follows", from = "K", to = "Y")
```

### Titles

If you want to add a title, set `main`, and style it with `style_title()`, which
takes the same fields as `style_labels()`:

  | Argument / field | Default                  | Controls                            |
  | ---------------- | ------------------------ | ----------------------------------- |
  | `main`           | `NULL`                   | plot title; `NULL` means no title   |
  | `fontsize`       | `14`                     | title font size                     |
  | `col`            | `"black"`                | title color                         |
  | `fontface`       | `"bold"`                 | title font face                     |
  | `title_gap`      | `grid::unit(1, "lines")` | gap between the title and the graph |

```{r}
#| label: title

cgraph_plot(dag, main = "My DAG") |>
  style_title(fontsize = 20, col = "navy")
```

## Figure size and margins

  | Argument       | Default               | Controls                                                       |
  | -------------- | --------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
  | `outer_margin` | `grid::unit(2, "mm")` | padding around the whole plot                                  |
  | `asp`          | `NA`                  | y/x aspect ratio of the layout; `NA` fills the available space |

A plot is drawn into whatever graphics device is open, so the figure size is set
the usual R way, e.g. with `grDevices::png(width =, height =)` or a chunk's
`fig-width`/`fig-height`. Let's make the figure a bit larger:

```{r}
#| label: fig-size
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6

cgraph_plot(dag)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Large graphs need a bigger figure"}
The default figure size works well for small examples. As your graph gets
larger, labels and edges can become cramped or overlap. Increase the figure size
(and, if needed, the node `radius` or the label `fontsize`) to keep larger
graphs readable.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Uneven figure sizes and `asp`"}
By default, node positions are stretched to fill the figure, which can distort
the layout's own proportions in an uneven figure. If you want to keep them
instead, set `asp = 1`.
:::

## Composing into an existing figure

So far each plot has had its own page. If you already have a grid viewport (for
example, as one panel of a larger figure), you can print a plot with
`newpage = FALSE` to draw it there instead.

Let's use this to draw the DAG and the ADMG side by side in one figure:

```{r}
#| label: existing-figure
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4

grid::grid.newpage()
grid::pushViewport(grid::viewport(layout = grid::grid.layout(1, 2)))
grid::pushViewport(grid::viewport(layout.pos.col = 1))
print(cgraph_plot(dag), newpage = FALSE)
grid::popViewport()
grid::pushViewport(grid::viewport(layout.pos.col = 2))
print(style_nodes(admg, fill = "salmon"), newpage = FALSE)
grid::popViewport()
```

## Combining options

Here we combine some of the styling above to plot a PAG:

```{r}
#| label: combined
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5

pag <- cgraph(
  "C o-> X, D --> G + Y, X --> D + F, Y --> H, K o-> X, K --> Y",
  class = "PAG"
)

cgraph_plot(pag, layout = "stress", main = "A cool PAG") |>
  style_nodes(fill = "whitesmoke", col = "slategray") |>
  style_nodes(fill = "skyblue", col = "royalblue", nodes = "X") |>
  style_nodes(fill = "gold", col = "darkorange", nodes = "Y") |>
  style_nodes(shape = "square", linestyle = "dashed", nodes = "K") |>
  style_edges(col = "darkslategray") |>
  style_edges(col = "royalblue", lty = "dashed", type = c("o->", "<-o")) |>
  style_edges(curvature = 0.3, from = "K", to = "Y") |>
  style_edges(label = "cool", from = "K", to = "X") |>
  style_labels(col = "navy", nodes = "X") |>
  style_labels(col = "saddlebrown", nodes = "Y") |>
  style_title(fontsize = 18, col = "navy")
```
